title: Part I — COMMERCE: What a Commerce Platform Is
basis: Reconstructed on 2026-11-12 from the published page (posts/part-1-intro/index.md, 451 words, ten units) and its former spec.md, then reordered the same day (see decision_log); the page was revised to match. One spec paragraph per unit of the page; the KEY POINTS callout and the three figures are evidence of the paragraph they stand with (Figure 3 with the roadmap, p04).

know: Part I answers five questions in order: what happens to an order, who sells what to whom, what the parts are, who owns each fact, and what the market sells.
can_do: Pick the Part I chapter that answers the decision in front of them.

audience.who: Readers new to commerce architecture in their first weeks at a merchant, a vendor or an agency (engineers, product managers and leaders) who have read the preface and are about to start Part I, or who arrive with one decision in hand and want the chapter that answers it.
already_knows: What buying something online is like from the shopper's side.
Roughly what an API, a database and a queue are.
The preface's claim that a commerce platform is the set of systems that make and keep promises (introduction).
Kestrel & Pine in outline: a fictional outdoor brand, its thirteen systems, its incidents, Noor Visser and the Waypoint program (meet-kestrel-and-pine).
does_not_know: Shop platform, as the book's name for the hosted product that runs the webshop (defined in journey-of-an-order).
Writer, capability, record and copy, scale stage, platform category: each is owned by a Part I chapter and is only named or glossed in a clause here.
Eva's order as the journey's worked example.

acceptance_criteria.expected: Order journey; business models; capability map; ownership of facts; platform landscape.

acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this page: why does this part start with the chapter that follows one order, and end with the chapter on what the market sells?

thesis.question: What is a commerce platform, before any technology is chosen?
thesis.claim: A commerce platform is the whole set of systems that make and keep promises to a customer, and nearly every commerce failure is a promise one system made and another could not keep.
thesis.disputed_by: The everyday meaning of 'commerce platform' as the product a merchant buys to run its web shop.
thesis.so_what: A merchant that treats the platform as one product looks for failures inside that product and replaces it; a merchant that sees the set of systems looks at the joins and fixes ownership.
thesis.how_why: The storefront makes the promises in seconds while the warehouse, carrier, payment provider and finance system keep them over days, each from its own copy of the facts.

supporting_claims.claim: An order is a chain of promises handed from system to system, and it breaks at the handoffs.
Who sells what to whom decides which promises are made and therefore which systems are needed.
The platform is a map of capabilities, each owning one kind of fact, and no vendor covers the whole map.
For each fact exactly one system must be the record; every other value is a copy.
Buying a platform moves the integration work to a different owner; it does not remove it.

role.contribution: Performs the part's opening: states the part thesis and the reading order.

additional_patterns.applies_to: chapters: the five chapter paragraphs, in the part's reading order

flow.rationale: The page opens on one shopper's order as the hook, to which the closing returns, and then narrows from the part's claim, to the one company the claim is tested on, to the five questions that take that company apart, to one paragraph per chapter, and ends on what the five answers add up to and where to start. The company stands before the chapter list because the chapter paragraphs name its cases and its Waypoint program, and each introduces its own person (Eva, Noor Visser) in a clause; the five questions stand directly before the list because they are the principle that orders it; the reading advice comes last because a reader can choose a chapter only after seeing what each one decides. Put the list first and Kestrel & Pine and Waypoint arrive unexplained; put the five questions before the company and they have nothing to be asked of; put the advice first and it points at chapters the reader has not met.

hook.content: A shopper places one order, but the warehouse, carrier, payment provider and finance team each have work to do before it is complete.

bridge.from_reader_world: The reader's experience as a shopper: one click, one confirmation, one order.
bridge.to_topic: The merchant's side of that order, where the storefront's promises about product, price, stock, delivery and returns depend on answers from other systems; hence the question of what a commerce platform is.

thesis_statement.text: Part I argues that a commerce platform is the whole set of systems that make and keep those promises, and that nearly every failure is a promise one system made and another could not keep. The product a merchant buys to run its webshop, the shop platform, is only one of them.
thesis_statement.placement: KEY POINTS bullet 1 and paragraph p02

promises.promise: Five chapters answer five questions in order: what happens to an order, who sells what to whom, what the parts of a platform are, who owns each fact, and what the market sells.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: One order placed by a shopper is finished only when the warehouse, the carrier, the payment provider and the finance team have each done their work, so the storefront's promises depend on systems the shopper never sees.

evidence.what: One order: the storefront promises product, price, stock, delivery and returns; the warehouse, carrier, payment provider and finance team have work to do before it is complete.
evidence.shows: The promise is made in one place and kept in others, which is the situation the part's claim explains.

evidence.what: Figure 1: a ticket of promises carried from the online shop to a warehouse, a delivery van, a payment terminal and a ledger.
evidence.shows: The storefront writes the promises in seconds; the other systems have to honour them over days.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Part I's claim: a commerce platform is the whole set of systems that make and keep those promises, of which the product that runs the webshop (the shop platform) is only one, and nearly every failure is a promise one system made and another could not keep; knowing who keeps each promise locates a failure.

evidence.what: Figure 2: the order's journey as a chain of promises, the storefront making them early and the other systems keeping them late.
evidence.shows: Every arrow is a handoff that can be late, lost, duplicated or misread, which is where the claim locates failures.

transition_in.carries_over: The one order and the storefront's promises that other systems must keep.
transition_in.introduces: The claim the part draws from it and the name 'shop platform' for the product that is only one of those systems.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The part tests the claim on Kestrel & Pine, a fictional outdoor brand whose thirteen systems hold orders and product data in four places each and let six writers (systems or people) change warehouse stock, and whose Waypoint program starts by deciding who owns what.

evidence.what: Kestrel & Pine (fictional): €48 million revenue in 2026, thirteen systems, 34 integrations, 41 apps; orders and product data each in four places; six writers of warehouse stock; Waypoint begins in March 2027.
evidence.shows: One merchant in which facts have several holders and no agreed owner: the claim's kind of failure, in numbers the chapters reuse.

transition_in.carries_over: The claim that failures are promises one system made and another could not keep.
transition_in.introduces: The one company on which every chapter of the part tests it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Part I examines that company with five questions in a fixed order (what happens to an order, who sells what to whom, what the parts are, who owns each fact, what the market sells), one chapter each, because each answer is the vocabulary the next question needs.

transition_in.carries_over: Kestrel & Pine's landscape and its unowned facts.
transition_in.introduces: The five questions the part asks of it, in order, and the reason for the order.

evidence.what: Figure 3: the five questions of Part I in reading order.
evidence.shows: Each answer is the vocabulary the next question needs, and together they are the reasoning behind Kestrel & Pine's 2027 decisions.

sections.heading: Chapters in this part
sections.controlling_idea: Each of the five chapters decides one question and tests the answer on one Kestrel & Pine case, and each builds on the chapter before it.

advances_thesis.how: Each paragraph introduces the chapter that argues one of the part's five supporting claims, so the list is the part's argument in outline.

additional_patterns.applies_to: p05 to p07: one order, then every way of selling, then the whole map

flow.rationale: The part's own reading order. The journey names the steps that the business models vary; the models say what a merchant must be able to do, which the capability map lays out; the map names the facts whose ownership the fourth chapter assigns; and only with jobs mapped and owners named can the reader judge what the market sells. Move the landscape chapter earlier and products are compared before the reader knows what they must do.

transition_in.introduces: One paragraph per chapter: the question in bold, what the chapter does with it and its Kestrel & Pine case.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Chapter 1 follows one purchase through thirteen steps, and its two orders show the normal path and why one status word cannot describe an order.

advances_thesis.how: Introduces the chapter that shows an order as a chain of handoffs.

evidence.what: Eva's jacket order (the normal path) and another order marked delivered, in picking and uninvoiced at once.
evidence.shows: The chapter works on concrete orders, and one of them cannot be explained by a single status.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Chapter 2 shows that the shape of the business decides the systems: with the same steps, who buys and through which channel changes who sets the price, who is the seller, who holds the stock and who ships; and as a merchant grows, its shape changes through four scale stages, by adding channels, stock locations, countries and brands rather than revenue.

advances_thesis.how: Introduces the chapter that ties the systems needed to who sells what to whom.

evidence.what: One jacket sold to a consumer, a wholesale customer, a marketplace customer or a store visitor.
evidence.shows: The product is constant, so the differences in who prices, sells, stocks and ships come from the buyer and the channel.

evidence.what: Four scale stages, from Starting to Group; a merchant moves between them by adding channels, stock locations, countries and brands, not by passing a revenue threshold.
evidence.shows: The stages are the same point over time: the shape of the business, not its size, decides the systems.

transition_in.carries_over: The thirteen steps of the journey, which stay the same.
transition_in.introduces: What changes around them with the buyer and the sales channel.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Chapter 3 maps the jobs a merchant must perform, which the book calls capabilities, before any software is chosen, and placing Kestrel & Pine's systems on that map exposes missing capabilities and overlapping writers.

advances_thesis.how: Introduces the chapter that draws the platform as a map of capabilities.

evidence.what: Head of Engineering Noor Visser places Kestrel & Pine's systems against the jobs.
evidence.shows: The map is a working tool: it shows what is missing and where several writers overlap.

transition_in.carries_over: The ways of selling, which say what a merchant must be able to do.
transition_in.introduces: The jobs themselves, laid out as a map before any software is chosen.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Chapter 4 assigns one authoritative owner to each fact, which the map alone cannot do when two systems hold the same fact and disagree.

advances_thesis.how: Introduces the chapter that separates the record of a fact from its copies.

evidence.what: Six competing answers about Kestrel & Pine's stock, one from each of the six writers named in p03, resolved in the worked example; systems meaning different things by 'order'.
evidence.shows: Disagreement between systems is the normal case the chapter resolves.

transition_in.carries_over: The capability map, which says which job should hold a fact.
transition_in.introduces: What the map cannot settle: two systems holding the same fact and disagreeing.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Chapter 5 comes last, once jobs are mapped and owners named: its seven platform categories differ less in features than in who hosts, upgrades and integrates, each moving the integration work rather than removing it, and two proposals to rebuild Kestrel & Pine's webshop end in keeping the shop platform and adding the missing capabilities.

advances_thesis.how: Introduces the chapter that shows a product moves integration work and does not remove it.

evidence.what: Two rebuild proposals tested against Kestrel & Pine's actual problems; the company keeps its shop platform and adds missing capabilities.
evidence.shows: A new product would not have solved problems of ownership.

evidence.what: Seven platform categories that differ in who hosts, upgrades and integrates, with dated evidence through 2026.
evidence.shows: The comparison rests on dated public evidence, sourced in that chapter.

transition_in.carries_over: The jobs mapped and the owners of facts named.
transition_in.introduces: What the market sells to do those jobs, and what it costs to operate.

conclusion.heading: Where to Begin
conclusion.synthesis: Kestrel & Pine's problems were facts nobody owned, at the handoffs between systems, which no replacement product would have fixed.
conclusion.so_what: A reader looks for a failure at the handoffs and asks who owns the fact before asking which product to buy.

callback.to: The shopper's one order of the opening (p01).
callback.how: Its promises are kept or broken at those handoffs, and the first chapter follows it through them.

takeaway.content: Read the chapters in order, beginning with the order's journey; with one decision to make, start at the chapter that answers it.

hand_off.carries_over: The part's claim that a commerce platform is the set of systems that make and keep promises.
hand_off.introduces: One order followed through thirteen steps, as the concrete case of that claim.

transition_in.carries_over: The five chapters and what each decides, ending with the company keeping its shop platform.
transition_in.introduces: What that outcome shows and where to start reading.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Kestrel & Pine's problems are unowned facts at the handoffs, where the shopper's one order breaks and which no product fixes; read the chapters in order from the order's journey, or, with one decision to make, start at the chapter that answers it.

non_goals.topic: Teaching any chapter's content; the page summarizes and does not re-argue.
